title: Opportunistic prefix clustering for KV shard sharing
creator: Maya Patel
description:
Problem: In bursty inference workloads we observe many requests with different prompts that nevertheless share semantically similar leading token sequences (templated prompts, repeated system messages, or slight user variations). The current KV cache is keyed by exact prefix signatures which leads to missed sharing opportunities and duplicated KV slices occupying GPU memory. This increases memory pressure and raises unit cost in Dedicated and Private deployments.

Proposal: Implement an opportunistic prefix clustering layer that groups similar prefixes into candidate clusters and then maps clusters to shared KV shards. The layer uses compact similarity sketches (SimHash / MinHash) combined with a lightweight LSH table to propose bucket matches at request time. When a cluster is accepted by the eviction/consistency policy, we materialize a single shared KV shard and a small redirection table so subsequent equivalent prefixes reuse the shard. The system is conservative by default: it only merges prefixes when sketch similarity >= threshold and when the projected memory win (in tokens) exceeds merge overhead.

Key design points and constraints: 1) Probabilistic similarity detection must not change model outputs: we never mutate KV content — merges only create shared pointers to the canonicalized KV slice. 2) Collisions must be handled deterministically across nodes: cluster IDs are derived from canonical sketch + epoch tag. 3) Runtime overhead per request must be <= 1% of current token-processing CPU overhead to preserve latency SLOs. 4) Safety: a roll-back path that splits shared shards if we detect a quality regression tied to a merge.

Implementation phases: Phase A (prototype) — generate sketches at prefix finalization, evaluate sketch collision rate on current traffic, offline cluster analysis using historical traces, and a sim workload to measure potential memory wins. Phase B (runtime guardian) — add a conservative merge executor in the host process that performs cluster acceptance and shard creation behind a feature flag. Phase C (canary + rollout) — run canary in a Dedicated pool, collect latency, cache-hit telemetry, and quality metrics tied to representative prompt testsets.

Motivation vs alternatives: Unlike aggressive compaction or exact canonicalization, clustering allows reuse across semantically similar but non-identical prompts (e.g., minor punctuation or name changes). Compared to global prefix canonicalization, the cluster approach avoids heavy upfront index maintenance and is compute-light at request time.

Metrics for success: reduced duplicated KV bytes on GPU, unchanged p50/p95 latency, no increase in generation regressions above noise floor.
acceptance_criteria: Prototype produces a sketch collision matrix for production traffic and a reproducible memory-win estimate
End-to-end integration reduces per-GPU KV memory used by >= 12% for workloads where similar-prefix density >= 20%
No measurable p50 latency regression (>+5ms) in canary runs
Automated split-on-regression path in runtime validated by tests
Instrumentation emits cluster-level telemetry (cluster_id, member_count, bytes_shared) and dashboard is wired
tasks: Create offline analyzer to compute similarity distributions from 14 days of inference traces
Implement compact sketch generator in runtime finalizer (C++ path + python test harness)
Build LSH candidate table with deterministic seeding and epoch tagging
Add merge executor behind feature flag; implement canonicalization pointer and redirection table
Write unit/integration tests verifying cluster deterministic behavior and split rollback
Benchmark memory/latency on Dedicated GPU pool with synthetic and sampled real workloads
Prepare canary plan and dashboard (SLOs: latency, token cost, correctness)
